label: proposition-state-independence
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{proposition-state-independence}
Suppose that a finite-mode Gaussian QMS admits a faithful normal invariant state. Then it admits a faithful normal Gaussian invariant state $ \sigma $. For each $ s \in [ 0, 1 ] $, the induced semigroup $ ( T_t^{ ( s ) } ) _{t \geq 0} $ on $ \mathcal{H} $ is independent of the choice of faithful normal invariant density. In particular, Theorem~\ref{theorem-all-s-representation} gives its second-quantization representation using $ \sigma $.

label: remark-reference-state
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remark-reference-state}
If the given invariant state $ \rho $ is non-Gaussian, the matrix $ \mathbf{S}_s $ is computed from the Gaussian reference state $ \sigma $. The unitary is constructed by replacing $ \rho $ with $ \sigma $ in \eqref{eq-all-s-unitary}, including the normalization by $ \chi_\sigma $. It sends the Fock vacuum to $ \sigma^{1/2} $. The Gaussian pairing identity is applied to this reference state; no such identity is asserted for the vectors $ \rho^{s/2} W ( z ) \rho^{ ( 1 - s ) /2} $ associated with a non-Gaussian $ \rho $. When the drift is stable, uniqueness of the invariant state gives $ \sigma = \rho $.
head: environment

label: theorem-main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theorem-main}
Let $ ( \mathcal{T}_t ) _{t \geq 0} $ be a Gaussian QMS on $ \mathcal{B} ( \Gamma ( \mathbb{C}^d ) ) $, with $ 1 \leq d < \infty $, admitting a faithful normal invariant state $ \rho $. The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item\label{condition-stable} The drift matrix $ \mathbf{Z} $ is stable.
\item\label{condition-unique} The semigroup has a unique normal invariant state.
\item\label{condition-kernel} For some $ s \in [ 0, 1 ] $, $ \ker L^{ ( s ) } $ is finite dimensional.
\item\label{condition-resolvent} For some $ s \in [ 0, 1 ] $, $ L^{ ( s ) } $ has compact resolvent.
\item\label{condition-one-time} For some $ s \in [ 0, 1 ] $ and some $ t > 0 $, $ T_t^{ ( s ) } $ is compact.
\item\label{condition-immediate} For every $ s \in [ 0, 1 ] $ and every $ t > 0 $, $ T_t^{ ( s ) } $ is compact.
\item\label{condition-trace-class} For every $ s \in [ 0, 1 ] $ and every $ t > 0 $, $ T_t^{ ( s ) } \in \mathcal{S}_1 ( \mathcal{H} ) $.
\end{enumerate}
If these conditions hold, $ \rho $ is Gaussian and $ \ker L^{ ( s ) } = \mathbb{C} \rho^{1/2} $ for every $ s $. If they fail, every $ \ker L^{ ( s ) } $ is infinite dimensional.
head: environment

label: lemma-infinite-fixed-space
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma-infinite-fixed-space}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{theorem-main}, if $ \mathbf{Z} $ is not stable, every $ \ker L^{ ( s ) } $ is infinite dimensional.

label: remark-no-general-equivalence
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remark-no-general-equivalence}
Reality of the Gaussian drift is essential in the proof of necessity. For a general complex one-particle generator, compact resolvent need not imply compactness of the semigroup. For example, on $ \Gamma ( \mathbb{C} ) $, the generator $ \mathrm{i} N = \lambda ( \mathrm{i} ) $ has compact resolvent because $ ( \lambda - \mathrm{i} n ) ^{ - 1} \to 0 $, whereas $ \Gamma ( \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} t} ) $ is unitary and noncompact. For a real Gaussian drift, each imaginary eigenvalue has its conjugate, which produces the infinitely many fixed tensors used in Lemma~\ref{lemma-infinite-fixed-space}.

label: remark-scope
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remark-scope}
The compactness argument uses finite dimensionality in two places: the operator norm is attained in the strict-contraction argument, and the finite-particle projections in \eqref{eq-chaos-tail} have finite rank. On an infinite-dimensional one-particle space, \cite[Theorem~3.10]{ArakiSinhaSunder1995} states that $ \Gamma ( B ) $ is compact if and only if $ B $ is compact and $ \norm{B} < 1 $. The same theorem characterizes trace-class and Hilbert--Schmidt membership by the corresponding membership of $ B $, together with $ \norm{B} < 1 $. In an infinite-mode setting, stability alone gives neither compactness of the one-particle semigroup nor the norm control used here. The compactness criterion of Theorem~\ref{theorem-main} is therefore specific to finitely many modes.
